find_chains.description: Search the EVM networks ChainList publishes, or browse them ranked by how much value is locked on them. Search by name, short name, chain ID or currency symbol: 'arbitrum', 'matic' and '8453' all work. Each network comes back with its chain ID, its currency, a working RPC endpoint and its block explorer, so the next step can use it without a second lookup. Test networks are included and labelled.
find_chains.name: find_chains

get_chain.description: Get everything ChainList holds about one network: its chain id in both decimal and hex, the coin gas is paid in, a working RPC endpoint, its block explorer, what it is built on and which bridges reach it. It also comes back with the five boxes a wallet's 'Add a network' form asks for, already filled in, so connecting a wallet is a copy rather than a hunt. Anything worth knowing first (a re-used chain id, a network still incubating) arrives as a warning rather than buried in a field.

get_explorer_links.description: Turn a transaction hash, a wallet address, a block number or a token contract into a link on the right block explorer for the network it is on: the link to put in the Slack message or the email. Leave the value empty to just list the explorers. Only explorers that promise a fixed link shape are linked into, so a link that comes back opens something rather than a 404, and a hash pasted where an address goes is caught here rather than at the explorer.

list_rpc_endpoints.description: Get the RPC endpoints published for one network, each with what its operator says it does with your requests. HTTPS by default, because that is what most things can call; switch to WebSocket for a subscription. Narrow to the operators that log little or nothing when the traffic is someone's. Endpoints ChainList lists but nothing can call (config-file templates, notes, bare hostnames) are left out, so every address that comes back is one you can use.

description: Look up any EVM network from a workflow. ChainList is the public registry of close to three thousand Ethereum-compatible networks: search them by name, chain ID or currency, get the settings a wallet needs to add one, pull a working RPC endpoint with its operator's logging policy attached, turn a transaction hash or a wallet address into a block explorer link, find the faucets for a test network, and see which layer 2s roll up to which network and over which bridges. Every action reads: nothing here changes anything. No account or API key is required.
